articles.title: The iPhone Duo Isn't Just Another Folding Phone
articles.content: Hello again, and welcome back to Fast Company ’s Plugged In . On Wednesday, Apple held its annual September product launch at its Steve Jobs Theater. The event will be remembered for two debuts. One was the long-awaited announcement of the company’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo . The other was the first public appearance of its new CEO , John Ternus, who appeared briefly in person and at length in the prerecorded keynote presentation. I came to Cupertino looking forward to the time I’d get with the folding iPhone in Apple’s post-keynote demo area. Though hardly enough to render a firm verdict on the device, that hands-on experience left me impressed with the thinking that Apple has put into the device. But I also left mulling over Ternus’s unexpectedly intriguing framing of the role that iPhones—folding or otherwise—play in the AI era. First, let’s talk about the Duo. By any measure, Apple is an exceptionally late arrival to the folding-screen party. Unlike the 2007 iPhone, the Duo is not a ground-up reimagining of a product category. Instead, it sits squarely in the same class as existing folding phones from Samsung and other makers of Android phones. Even its distinctive, passport-like form factor, with a squat outer screen and an inner one optimized for full-screen video, had some of its thunder purloined when Samsung announced the similar Galaxy Z Fold8 six weeks earlier. Yet the Duo, which is entering the market more than seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy folding phone , is fully baked in ways other companies’ early folding phones were not. While other companies were putting their models through iteration after iteration , Apple was waiting until it had good answers to the myriad questions presented by the form factor. Such as: What size and aspect ratio should the inner and outer screens be? Which things about iOS’s user interface do and don’t need to change to accommodate those two displays? How do you minimize the crease at the folding point so users don’t obsess over it every time they open their phone? Overall, Apple’s design decisions appear to strike a maximally happy balance between the Duo’s two screen sizes, something other folding phones long struggled with. In a daring change to a basic aspect of iOS, Apple repositioned the dock and other toolbars to the screens’ right edge. That helps prevent apps from merely stretching out to fill more space, an issue that can leave Android-based folding phones (and tablets) feeling like they don’t deliver on the promise of their extra display acreage. The iPhone Duo’s screen aspect ratios strike a balance other makers of folding phones have struggled to reach. [Photo: Apple] When it came to facilitating the use of multiple apps on the inner screen, Apple didn’t invent a whole new mode of interaction. Instead, it pretty much revived the split-view multitasking that the iPad had until last year, when the company ditched it for a more Mac-like interface. I find the iPad’s new system an overcomplication rather than an improvement —which seems to be a minority view—and welcome the return of the old approach’s streamlined simplicity on the Duo. As for that pesky crease, Apple’s solution involves giving the inner screen a “nano-texture” matte finish that cuts glare, reducing the telltale reflections the fold would otherwise have. It’s a clever work-around that adds to the Duo’s generally posh vibe. Speaking of posh, there’s the unavoidable subject of the phone’s price. At $1,999 for the 256 GB version, it’s less than many analysts expected . But there’s no getting around the fact that it makes the Duo either unaffordable or a serious splurge for most people. Girding yourself to buy one may be easiest if you’d otherwise purchase both a new iPhone ($699 and way, way up) and an iPad Mini (at least $599). The Duo’s price might also make more sense if you embrace its transformer-style nature. You can prop it up like a tent for movie watching or open it into a laptop-esque clamshell for hands-free video calls. Or you can unfold it all the way and use the larger screen while the smaller one on the other side lets photo subjects see themselves, brings a nearby friend into FaceTime sessions, or shows Snoopy animations to focus the attention of a kid whose picture you’re taking. Apple has been clever with these scenarios, and it’s fun to think of additional ones it could add over time. Judged strictly on what it does and how it does it, the Duo appears to validate Apple’s why-rush-things attitude toward foldability. Its potential is constrained by its price more than its appeal, but it won’t be surprising if it meaningfully boosts the sales of folding phones all by itself. (They currently account for just 2% of the market .) Now, on to Ternus’s remarks during the keynote. Nobody was expecting him to articulate a vision for Apple that boldly departed from that of his predecessor, Tim Cook. He didn’t. Still, I detected signs of his background as a product guy. Cook’s keynote comments on what Apple was trying to do usually didn’t go much beyond saying that it wanted to make great products that people love. Ternus, by contrast, immediately began explaining the iPhone’s role in people’s lives—a task that wouldn’t have been necessary until AI upended the entire tech industry. AI, he argued, “can become even more useful when it brings together your life with the apps, services, and products you use every day. And this means the product at the center of your experiences becomes even more essential. What I like to think of as an intelligent personal hub. It’s the intersection of your personal context that makes this idea so powerful.” Then Ternus listed the features you’d want in such a hub: a powerful processor, pervasive networking, a beautiful display, cameras, microphones, long battery life, and the ability to work seamlessly with other devices, apps, and services. “In other words, you would arrive at something remarkably familiar. Because there’s no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone.” Not everyone attempting to invent the next generation of AI gadgetry would agree. Many of them are predicated on the assumption that the smartphone era has left people weary of all the screens in their lives. OpenAI, for example, is reportedly readying a screenless, puck-sized speaker. And then there’s the iPhone Duo. It’s . . . a smartphone! With two screens! Apple is betting that a critical mass of people are not tired of smartphones. Instead, they crave one that’s even more capable, because it’s capable of displaying more information. (The Duo’s inner screen is 50% larger than that of the iPhone 18 Max.) But wait. Along with the iPhone Duo, Apple’s Wednesday event featured the announcement of the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. Among their features is an AI-powered mode that can listen to conversations, summarize them, and even let you see a text recap of the last 15 seconds. The Apple Watch does have a screen, of course, but this new capability offers a minimalist, ambient form of AI that wouldn’t work if it involved taking a phone out of your pocket. A product Apple didn’t announce on Wednesday is also relevant here: AirPods Pro with built-in cameras . Now expected next year , they appear to offer a visual counterpart to the new Apple Watch’s audio AI. Rather than letting you capture snapshots or video, they’ll feed imagery to Apple Intelligence for analysis. The new Apple Watch audio features have been greeted with skepticism over the propriety of a smartwatch capturing the speech of people who might not be aware that it’s listening. Some folks are already in a tizzy over the privacy implications of AirPods that can see. If Apple convinces people that these new features can’t be used for untoward purposes, the seamless, multi-device AI Ternus talked about could start to look very real. It would be tough for other companies to match. As Ternus introduced the concept of the iPhone as intelligent personal hub, he didn’t mention the iPhone Duo or new Apple Watches—they weren’t unveiled until later in the keynote—let alone the still-unannounced AirPods Pro. But his use of the term reminded me of another moment of truth, more than 25 years ago, when Steve Jobs pointed Apple toward the future by calling its most popular product a hub. In January 2001, Jobs was a fairly new CEO himself—it had been only a year since he’d stripped the “interim” from that title after returning to the company he’d cofounded . Apple was still bouncing back from the late-1990s turmoil that had threatened its very existence. The bulbous, all-in-one iMac was already a hit. But computers of all kinds were feeling somewhat outdated, at least in comparison to newer devices such as MP3 players, digital cameras, DV camcorders, and PDAs. That’s when Jobs used a Macworld Expo keynote to position the Mac as something new: a digital hub that would help you get more out of all those new gizmos in your life. The company already had a tool for editing video, iMovie. It began to roll out more media apps, such as iTunes and iDVD. Eventually, it released a whole suite of them called iLife. Apple didn’t have to make the case for the Mac being a digital hub for long. Mostly, it just made sure it was a great one. The strategy was central to the Mac’s rebound and led to the company releasing its own MP3 player, the iPod. Without the iPod, there might not have been an iPhone. Without the iPhone, who knows what Apple would look like today? Ternus’s intelligent personal hub might have a similar trajectory: something that begins as a new way of looking at Apple’s products and then redefines them so successfully that it no longer has to be acknowledged. Back when Jobs pitched the idea of the Mac as a digital hub, he wasn’t just talking about the iMac. Apple made many Macs, from PowerBooks and iBook laptops to the budget-priced Mac Mini to hulking Power Mac desktops to the memorable failure known as the G4 Cube . If the iPhone is going to be an intelligent personal hub, different people will want different expressions of the idea. And the iPhone Duo—the most different iPhone that Apple has made since the original—may be a clue to Ternus’s larger vision for the company’s future. "무료 빅데이터 교육부터 직무능력인증서·이수 이벤트까지" 고려사이버대학교 미래교육원(원장 이은택)은 교육부가 주관하는 매치업(Match業) 프로그램의 일환으로 '빅데이터 실무전문가 기초과정' 수강생을 상시 모집한다고 밝혔다. 이번 과정은 전액 무료로 운영되며, 일정 기준을 충족한 학습자에게는 교육부가 인정하는 '기초직무능력인증서'가 발급된다. 매치업은 신산업 분야의 직무능력 향상을 지원하는 단기 교육과정이다. 대학생과 구직자, 재직자 등 빅데이터 분야에 관심 있는 사람이라면 누구나 참여할 수 있다. 학습자는 과정을 통해 산업 현장에서 요구되는 실무 역량을 체계적으로 습득하고, 직무능력인증서를 통해 해당 역량을 공식적으로 인정받을 수 있다. 고려사이버대학교는 데이터 전문기업 ㈜데이터스트림즈와 컨소시엄을 구성해 빅데이터 분야의 실무 중심 교육과정을 공동 개발·운영하고 있다. 교육과정은 데이터 분석에 필요한 수학적 기초부터 실무 도구 활용까지 총 4개 트랙, 5개 강좌로 구성됐다. 단계별 학습을 통해 기초 이론과 데이터 분석 방법을 익히고, 이를 실제 업무에 적용할 수 있는 역량을 강화하는 데 초점을 맞췄다. 기초직무능력인증서는 과정별로 2개 과목 이상을 이수한 학습자에게 발급된다. 과목별로 과제와 퀴즈, 시험 등 평가 점수 합계가 60점 이상이면 이수 기준을 충족한다. 인증서는 매치업 대표기업인 ㈜데이터스트림즈와 국가평생교육진흥원 명의로 발급되며, 과정 이수 후 익월부터 발급받을 수 있다. 매치업 공식 사이트에서도 인증서 발급이 가능하다. 고려사이버대학교 미래교육원은 학습자의 과정 이수를 독려하기 위해 '이수 완료 이벤트'를 진행한다. 이벤트 참여 기간은 12월 13일까지다. 해당 기간에 매치업 기초과정 강좌를 이수한 후 공지사항에 게시된 구글폼을 통해 신청하면 된다. 이은택 고려사이버대학교 미래교육원장은 "이번 과정은 데이터 기반 사회에서 요구되는 실무 역량을 누구나 비용 부담 없이 습득할 수 있도록 기획됐다"며 "취업을 준비하는 학습자는 물론, 빅데이터 분야로의 직무 전환이나 역량 강화를 희망하는 재직자에게 실질적인 도움이 되기를 기대한다"고 말했다. 수강 신청은 K-MOOC 홈페이지 내 매치업 교육과정에서 '빅데이터' 분야 강좌를 선택해 진행할 수 있다. 이수 완료 이벤트의 세부 내용과 신청 방법은 해당 강좌 공지사항에서 확인할 수 있다. 한편, 고려사이버대학교는 2027학년도 1학기 일반대학원과 경영전문대학원 신입생을 11월 16일부터 모집한다. 직장인의 경우 산업체위탁 협약을 통해 등록금 30% 감면 혜택을 받을 수 있다. 모집 요강은 입학지원센터 홈페이지 및 대표전화를 통해 확인할 수 있다. 빅데이터실무전문가 과정 (고려사이버대학교 제공) 빅데이터실무전문가 기초과정 강좌소개 (고려사이버대학교 제공) <이 기사는 대학에서 제공한 정보기사로, 한겨레의 의견과 다를 수 있습니다>
articles.summary: Korea Cyber University's Future Education Center is continuously enrolling students for its 'Big Data Specialist Basic Course,' approved by the Ministry of Education. This program directly addresses the critical shortage of skilled professionals in data analytics and ICT, providing essential training for the burgeoning digital economy. By making specialized big data education accessible, South Korea is proactively building a robust workforce capable of leveraging advanced analytics for innovation and economic growth, setting a national benchmark for workforce development in the AI era.

articles.title: VAR Fails Manchester Derby, Haaland Goal Mistakenly Awarded
articles.summary: The Premier League's refereeing body has publicly admitted a significant VAR error in awarding Erling Haaland's decisive goal in the Manchester derby, directly impacting the game's outcome. This mistake underscores the persistent challenges and ethical questions surrounding the implementation of technology in high-stakes sports, particularly when human judgment remains the ultimate arbiter. The incident reignites debates about the reliability and efficacy of VAR, impacting fan confidence and the integrity of professional sports.

articles.title: Fable 5.1 Solves 370-Year-Old Cipher
articles.summary: Fable 5.1, a specialized software, has achieved a significant breakthrough by successfully decrypting the Cyphral Distich, a 370-year-old historical cipher. This accomplishment demonstrates the formidable power of modern computational tools in unlocking historical mysteries that have long eluded human analysis. The decryption not only provides new insights into historical communication methods but also showcases the capabilities of advanced algorithms in solving complex cryptographic challenges, opening new avenues for historical and linguistic research.
